grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: Moja torba; twoja torba. Ala trzyma swoją torbę. Jan trzyma swoją torbę.

tables.caption: Moja torba → moją torbę
rows: W mojej torbie jest moje narzędzie.

tables.caption: Ala; Jan → swoją torbę
rows: Jan pokazuje ołówek w swojej torbie.

grammar.note_en:
A possessive identifies whose thing we mean. Mój means “my”, twój means “your” when speaking to one familiar person, and nasz means “our”. Ala says To jest moja torba, “This is my bag”; Jan then says To jest moja torba about a different bag. My changes its reference when the speaker changes. When Ala speaks to Jan, twoja torba is “your bag”, Jan’s red bag. A bag is a torba; rzecz is the more general “thing” or “belonging”. The white bag and the large tool are both things, but only one is a bag.

Ownership and holding are different. Jan first takes the white bag and mistakenly calls it his. Ala’s statement and Jan’s own red contact label correct him. Trzymam twoją torbę means “I am holding your bag”: Jan holds it, but Ala owns it. The large tool is also Ala’s. Later a small tool is found inside her bag, and she explicitly says To nie jest moje narzędzie, “This is not my tool”. Being inside someone’s bag does not prove ownership. The hammer receives an explicit joint claim by Ala and Jan: nasz młotek, “our hammer”. Ewa’s use or inspection of it would not make her an owner. Nasz describes a shared relationship; the hammer is still one singular object, so no plural noun or new plural verb ending follows from this word.

Agreement means matching a describing word to its noun. A possessive agrees with the thing identified, rather than the sex of its owner. Mój ołówek is “my pencil” with a masculine noun; moja torba is “my bag” with a feminine noun; moje narzędzie is “my tool” with a neuter noun. Ala can say mój ołówek and Jan can say moja torba: the noun determines the ending. Twój follows the same three-way distinction in twój dom, “your home”, twoja torba, “your bag”, and twoje narzędzie, “your tool”. These are singular forms. Moje narzędzie does not mean several tools.

Case also changes the ending. A case is the form a word takes for its job in a sentence. Naming uses nominative moja torba, “my bag”. A positive direct object, the thing someone takes or holds, uses accusative moją torbę, “my bag”. The possessive and noun both change. In Trzymam twoją torbę, “I am holding your bag”, twoją likewise matches accusative torbę. Neuter moje narzędzie and masculine inanimate mój ołówek keep the same surface form as objects in these examples. The forms taught here do not supply every case of every possessive.

A negated direct object takes genitive: Nie trzymam mojej torby means “I am not holding my bag”. Mojej matches torby. Jan nie bierze naszego młotka means “Jan is not taking our hammer”; naszego matches młotka. Jan nie czyta swojego adresu means “Jan is not reading his own address”; swojego matches adresu. Contrast To nie jest moje narzędzie, “This is not my tool”. This is a negated naming sentence, not a negated direct object, so it retains nominative moje narzędzie. Do not change every word after nie to genitive.

Static place phrases keep the already taught locative: w mojej torbie means “in my bag”, w twojej torbie “in your bag”, and w swojej torbie “in his/her own bag” according to the subject. In Pracuję z moim przyjacielem, “I am working with my friend”, z takes the accompaniment instrumental and moim matches przyjacielem. My friend expresses a personal relationship, not ownership of a person. This chapter adds possessive agreement to cases already met; it does not introduce recipient, direction or source constructions.

Swój means “one’s own” and normally points back to the subject of its clause, the person doing the action. In Ala bierze swoją białą torbę, “Ala takes her own white bag”, Ala is the subject and owner. In Jan bierze swoją czerwoną torbę, “Jan takes his own red bag”, Jan is the subject and owner. The form swoją is unchanged because each object is a feminine accusative bag; the owner changes with the subject. Jan bierze swój ołówek means “Jan takes his own pencil”. Ala bierze swoje duże narzędzie means “Ala takes her own large tool”. In Jan pokazuje ołówek w swojej torbie, “Jan shows the pencil in his own bag”, swojej refers to Jan even though ołówek is nearer to it. Look for the subject, not the closest noun or the person who last held the object.

Mój and twój refer to speaker and addressee; swój refers to the grammatical subject. Their uses can overlap when that subject is the speaker or addressee. Mam swoją torbę is the usual neutral “I have my own bag”. Mam moją torbę can also be meaningful, especially when contrasting my bag with yours. The story’s mistaken claim uses moją and its correction uses swoją; this is an ownership correction, not proof that moją is always ungrammatical. Form exercises supply the possessive family to practise its ending. Vocabulary exercises restrict choices by a visible bank and sense cue. Open answers accept truthful variants rather than rejecting mój or twój solely because a subject also allows swój. Swój is a possessive here; no reflexive object pronoun is being taught.

Dom means “home” or “house”. Jan draws his home on a fresh sheet, separate from the older city/street sketch. Adres means “address”. His red bag has his reported contact label Łódź — ulica Biała, “Łódź — Biała Street”. The small unfamiliar tool bears a different old label, Łódź — ulica Lipowa, “Łódź — Lipowa Street”. Each label gives a city and street, without a number. A contact address does not prove legal ownership of a house, and the old tool label does not identify its present owner or location of origin. Irena’s Nie pamiętam adresu, “I do not remember the address”, concerns that old address, not a failure to remember her own home address. The lamp and original key remain unclaimed.

Czy Jan rysuje ___, nie stół?
Ala mówi: duże narzędzie to moja ___.

obrazec.prompt: Ala mówi: Ewa nie bierze ___ młotka.
obrazec.rule: Wyrazy: moją, twoje, nasz, swojej, moim, swój, naszego. 5: my; 6: your; 7: our; 8: own; Przykład: our.

items.prompt: Ala mówi: Jan trzyma ___ białą torbę.
Jan pyta: czy Ewa pokazuje ___ narzędzie?
Ala mówi: tu na podłodze jest ___ młotek.
Jan widzi ołówek w ___ czerwonej torbie.
„Moja torba”: co jest w białej torbie?
items.model_answer: W białej torbie jest duże narzędzie.
items.rubric: Name Ala’s large tool in a full sentence. The bag and large tool receive her explicit claims. The unfamiliar small tool has not yet been revealed; do not identify the original key or lamp as hers.

items.prompt: Jan mówi: „Mam moją torbę.” Co trzyma Jan?
items.rubric: At the mistake Jan holds Ala’s white bag, not his own red one. A truthful fuller answer can distinguish holding from ownership; Jan’s corrected twoją is addressed to Ala.

items.prompt: „Masz moją torbę”: co mówi Ala?
items.rubric: Give Ala’s explicit shared hammer claim in a full sentence. Nasz includes Ala and Jan here, not Ewa. A truthful quote about her own bag is also valid if the claimed object is identified.

items.prompt: „Swój ołówek”: co bierze Jan?
items.rubric: Jan takes his own original pencil, or his own red bag at the preceding action. Swój follows Jan as subject. Truthful naming with mój in Jan’s quoted speech or a full sentence identifying the red bag is also acceptable.

items.prompt: „Swój ołówek”: co mówi Ala?
items.rubric: The small unfamiliar tool is not Ala’s according to her statement, even though it is in her white bag. Identify this contrast in a full sentence; do not infer Ewa owns it because she holds it.

items.prompt: „Stary adres”: co czyta Ewa?
items.rubric: Name the old city/street label on the small tool. Keep it distinct from Jan’s Łódź — ulica Biała contact label. No street number, present owner, source or lamp connection is established.

items.prompt: Co jest w twojej torbie?
items.rubric: Answer truthfully in your own sentence using a demonstrated singular noun. The model is only an example. If you do not have a bag, Nie mam mojej torby is a valid negative answer; another truthful demonstrated sentence is valid. Do not require the learner to invent an address or ownership claim.
